text:
A: Hello. Erm, can you hear me?
B: Yes. Hello.
A: I'm Annelies. I'm in Sheffield.
B: Shahida. Ilford. East London.
A: Nice to meet you. How did you, erm, how did you find the puzzle?
B: It was ok. Some of them was too fiddly. I do these surveys a lot, they always have a puzzle.
A: Oh, so you've done a few of these, then.
B: Many. For the vouchers. Amazon vouchers. My grandson wants trainers, so.
A: That's very practical.
B: You have to be. Price of everything going up. Lamb I bought last week, two pound more than before. Same butcher, same lamb.
A: Yes, the shopping is shocking at the moment. I've noticed it with butter especially.
B: You are not from here? Your accent.
A: No, I'm Dutch, originally. From Amersfoort, near Utrecht. But I've been in Sheffield more than thirty years now. My husband's English, we met on a walking holiday.
B: Thirty years. Me, I came in 1978. From Lahore. So we are both, you know, from somewhere else.
A: Yes. Sometimes I still feel a bit foreign, to be honest. Even after all this time.
B: Hm. I don't think about it. My house is here, my children here, that's it. We own our house, no mortgage, since long time.
A: That must be a good feeling.
B: Very good. My husband wanted to spend on a new car, I said no, first the house.
A: Sensible. Erm, do you have children nearby?
B: Three, all married. Elder son is ten minutes from me, Gants Hill. His children I pick up from school two days a week, I give them dinner. Proper food, not chicken nuggets. Their mother, she, acha, she is busy.
A: How old are they?
B: Seven and five. The little one is very naughty, but clever. He can do my phone better than me.
A: They always can. Mine are grown up now, a son in Leeds and a daughter in Bristol. No grandchildren yet. My sister in Utrecht has grandchildren, she sends me photos every Sunday.
B: Bristol is far, for a daughter.
A: It is. She lives on her own. I worry, erm, more than I should, probably.
B: Mothers always worry. What you do for work?
A: I'm an executive assistant at the university here. For the head of a faculty. Diary, committee papers, that sort of thing.
B: Office. I worked in a shop, Green Street, ladies' suits and fabric. Fifteen years. Stopped at sixty, knees.
A: Oh, that's a lot of standing.
B: All day standing. And customers wanting discount, discount. I never gave too much.
A: I can believe that.
B: You cook? Your kitchen looked tidy, in the picture.
A: Oh, thank you. Yes, I cook most evenings. Soup, or stamppot, that's a Dutch thing, potatoes mashed with vegetables. And I bake an apple cake for church.
B: Potatoes with vegetables, ok. I make aloo, same idea, more spice.
A: Quite a lot more spice, I imagine.
B: Much more. That's it, I think time is nearly finished.
